- Intermittent mucus in stool (reported in up to half of microscopic colitis cases)  
- No hematochezia, melena, weight loss, fever, or night sweats (aligns with microscopic colitis, not IBD or infection)  
- Mild leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance (seen in subset of microscopic colitis due to mucosal T-cell infiltration and low-grade inflammation)  
- Normal hemoglobin (microscopic colitis does not cause anemia unless severe/chronic, which is absent here)  
- Pending colonoscopy and biopsies (diagnostic gold standard for microscopic colitis — requires random colonic biopsies even if endoscopy appears normal)

[GAPS]  
- Fecal calprotectin result (critical: normal or mildly elevated calprotectin occurs in microscopic colitis, but a clearly elevated value would favor IBD)  
- Colonoscopy findings and histopathology (definitive diagnosis requires biopsy-proven intraepithelial lymphocytosis ≥20/100 epithelial cells [lymphocytic] or subepithelial collagen band >10 µm [collagenous])  
- CRP and ESR (to assess systemic inflammation — typically normal/mildly elevated in microscopic colitis vs. often elevated in active IBD)  
- Stool studies (C. difficile NAAT, ova & parasite, Giardia/Cryptosporidium PCR) — to exclude chronic infection mimicking microscopic colitis  
- Celiac serology (tTG-IgA + total IgA) — celiac can rarely present with similar histology (e.g., increased intraepithelial lymphocytes), requiring differentiation

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Microscopic colitis
